strengths: Formulating 3D scene layout generation as an RL optimization problem using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) without relying exclusively on fixed ground-truth layouts is a conceptually neat idea.
The hybrid reward formulation combines structural validity (format), geometric/physical plausibility (collision and boundary checks), and perceptual/aesthetic quality via rendered views.
The paper is generally well-structured and easy to follow.
weaknesses: Absence of essential baselines: The paper repeatedly argues that Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is inadequate for 3D layout generation due to the lack of unique ground truth, yet provides no empirical comparison against an SFT baseline. Furthermore, competitive prior works mentioned in the text (e.g., LayoutGPT, LayoutVLM, LayoutDreamer) are not benchmarked.

Severely underspecified experimental setup: Section 3.1 states only that models were trained on 'a curated dataset of indoor 3D scenes', without disclosing the dataset source (e.g., 3D-FRONT, SUN RGB-D), number of training/test scenes, object asset origins, or split sizes. Training hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, number of GRPO iterations, rollout samples) are completely omitted.

Practicality and cost of online rendering and GPT-4o evaluation: The framework proposes rendering layouts with Blender and querying GPT-4o for reward evaluation during RL exploration. Running multi-turn rollouts (G trajectories × T turns) with API-based visual LLM scoring in the loop typically introduces extreme latency and financial cost; the paper lacks any discussion, cost analysis, or runtime details regarding this.

Absolute performance remains weak: In Table 1, the best model (Qwen 7B + MetaSpatial) still suffers from a 76.2% constraint violation ratio (and 100% on the 3B model), meaning more than three-quarters of objects violate spatial constraints. The reasons for such high failure rates are not critically analyzed.

Rough draft quality and typos: The abstract cuts off mid-sentence ('available at [blank]'); Figure 2 contains very small, low-resolution renderings without explanatory callouts; and Table 3 labels variants confusingly as 'Multi-turn RL (GRPO) w/o T = 1/3/5' instead of 'w/ T = 1/3/5'.

strengths: The motivation is clear and timely: leveraging reinforcement learning (specifically GRPO) to improve the 3D spatial reasoning and layout generation capabilities of vision-language models without relying on rigid ground-truth annotations.
The reward structure logically decomposes layout quality into format adherence, physical plausibility (collision and boundary checks), and perceptual/aesthetic quality.
The ablation experiments systematically examine the effect of each reward component and compare multi-turn trajectories against single-step optimization.
weaknesses: Critical lack of baseline comparisons: The method is only compared against the base Qwen models (with vs. without RL) and simple RL ablations (PPO). There are no comparisons against established 3D layout generation methods discussed in related work, such as LayoutGPT, LayoutVLM, or LayoutDreamer.

Severe omission of dataset and evaluation split details: Section 3.1 states only that models are trained on a 'curated dataset of indoor 3D scenes' without specifying the data source (e.g., 3D-FRONT), dataset size, diversity, or train/validation/test splits. It is unclear whether evaluation is performed on unseen scenes and unseen object sets.

Circular evaluation and potential reward hacking: GPT-4o is employed both as an online reward signal during RL training and as the primary metric for evaluating scene realism and aesthetic coherence. Evaluating on the exact reward model used for optimization introduces severe evaluation bias, and no independent human evaluation is provided.

Incomplete layout representation: The formulation predicts only positions (x, y, z) for objects. In 3D indoor scene layout, object orientation (yaw) and 3D bounding extents are essential; placing furniture without predicting orientation renders real-world utility limited.

Unsatisfactory residual error rates: Even after MetaSpatial optimization, the constraint violation ratio remains extremely high (76.2% for 7B and 100% for 3B), indicating persistent failure to satisfy room boundary and support constraints.

Drafting and presentation flaws: The abstract abruptly cuts off ('pipeline are publicly available at '), Figure 2 qualitative images are tiny and barely legible thumbnails, Table 3 mislabels trajectory length as 'w/o T=1/3/5' instead of 'w/ T=1/3/5', and several typographical errors appear throughout the text (e.g., 'RL s enables', 'inefficient of SFT').

strengths: Exploring reinforcement learning with multi-reward signals (syntax, physical collision, and visual assessment) for 3D layout generation is a relevant and timely research direction.
The paper includes ablations examining the impact of individual reward components (Table 2) and varying multi-turn refinement horizons (Table 3).
weaknesses: Incomplete submission and missing links: The abstract abruptly cuts off mid-sentence at 'Our code, data, and training pipeline are publicly available at', indicating an unpolished draft.

Absence of external baselines: Despite positioning the method against existing layout generation approaches (e.g., LayoutGPT, LayoutVLM, I-Design, SFT baselines), the paper only compares Qwen2.5-VL zero-shot against itself fine-tuned with the proposed method. Without evaluating standard benchmarks and representative prior works, the empirical claims cannot be substantiated.

Underspecified dataset and experimental protocol: Section 3.1 merely notes that models are trained on a 'curated dataset of indoor 3D scenes' without specifying the data source (e.g., 3D-FRONT), dataset size, train/validation/test splits, or how generalizability to novel rooms/assets is measured.

Questionable generation quality: Despite training, the physical constraint violation ratio remains alarmingly high at 76.2% for the 7B model and 100% for the 3B model, indicating that the vast majority of generated scenes remain physically invalid (e.g., out of bounds or floating objects).

Inadequate qualitative presentation: The renders shown in Figure 2 are tiny, low-resolution thumbnails without annotations, bounding boxes, or readable details, making it impossible to assess the visual and geometric claims made in the text.

Theoretical and algorithmic discrepancies in GRPO formulation: Equations (4) and (5) omit the group-relative standardization (subtracting group mean and dividing by standard deviation) that fundamentally defines Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Furthermore, discounting cumulative rewards using $\gamma^t$ with $t$ increasing penalizes later refinement turns, contradicting the intuition that multi-turn iterative refinement should optimize for the quality of the final layout.

Cost and reproducibility of online multimodal LLM-as-a-judge: Involving Blender rendering and live GPT-4o API calls within the inner RL rollout loop across multiple group samples and refinement steps is costly, slow, and non-deterministic, yet no analysis of computational budget, API costs, or reproducibility is provided.
